sections.h2: What the Lenawee County Register of Deeds does
sections.html:
The Register of Deeds in Adrian, the county seat, receives, records and digitally stores every legal document that affects real estate in Lenawee County. That covers deeds, land contracts, mortgages, liens, surveys and land corners. Staff check each item against Michigan's recording rules, record it, and send the original back by U.S. mail to whoever presented it unless instructed otherwise.

Whether a house stands near Adrian, in Tecumseh or on a farm road in a rural township, the deed goes to this one county office. Michigan leaves assessing, zoning and building rules to individual cities and townships, and keeps deed recording with the county. The legal description in the deed gives the exact boundaries. The county had 43,577 housing units at the 2020 census, and 77.3 percent of occupied homes were lived in by their owners.

The office supplies no forms, and its employees are barred from advising on or helping complete a document. Content and intent are the preparer's responsibility, so closings usually run through a title agent or a lawyer.

If you are preparing to sell, call the office with your parcel's legal description and ask what is of record. Staff can tell you whether the vesting deed, a mortgage or a lien shows up, though they cannot interpret what it means for your sale. That answer helps your title agent plan the closing, and it costs nothing to ask.

Recording runs $30.00 per document, whether it is one page or twenty. A page copy at the counter is $1.00. The counter takes checks, cash and cards, and cards carry an access fee.

Owners sometimes receive letters from commercial services offering certified copies of their deeds by mail for as much as $83.00 each. The identical record is available from the county's own counter for as little as $2.00. Call the office before paying a mailer.

The county posts 17 statutory requirements and treats them as a minimum, since some instruments carry extra rules. These are the ones that most often matter on a home sale:

  • Signatures must be original, with names typed or printed beneath, and those names must agree with the notary block (MCL 565.201).
  • Page one needs a 2.5 inch blank band across its upper edge, and all remaining edges need half an inch.
  • Use black ink in at least 10-point type on white 20-pound paper that is at least letter size and no longer than legal.
  • The first printed line has to state the recordable event, and one instrument may evidence only one event.
  • Include the grantee's street or post office address, plus drafter identification with a name and address.
  • A Michigan-signed deed needs acknowledgment by a judge, a court clerk or a notary public.
  • Social Security numbers may appear only as the final four digits.

A deed that says "survivor" must be backed by a certified death certificate that is recorded with it or already of record and cited by liber and page. A court order must carry the court clerk's certification and seal.

A rejected document is mailed back, and the closing waits until a corrected one is presented. Because the title agent normally handles this, ask early whether the deed has been checked against the list above, and read the notary block yourself before signing day.

sections.h2: Transfer tax on a house sale
sections.html:
On nearly every sale for money, tax is owed. Michigan's state transfer tax attaches to deeds given for consideration. Under MCL 207.523, the seller is the liable party, and the money is paid to the county treasurer for the parcel's location. A separate county transfer tax comes from Act 134 of 1966. Phone the Register of Deeds for the combined figure on your price. Closing agents ordinarily subtract it from the seller's proceeds.

The statutes also list transfers that escape the tax. A few that touch homeowners:

  • Deeds with consideration under $100.
  • Gifts of a home by an individual to a child or grandchild (state exemption, MCL 207.526).
  • Court orders that move title without naming a price.
  • Corrective quitclaim deeds that only fix a defect in title.
  • Land contracts, until legal title actually passes.
  • Mortgage foreclosures and the deeds that replace them.

Any exemption you claim must be cited correctly in the deed itself, so run the citation past your closing agent.

sections.h2: Searching land records in Adrian and around the county
sections.html:
The county offers an online search with two doors. A text search reads typed or legible text and works on a phone. A second tool serves experienced users and searches by name, recorded date, and liber and page. It runs best on a computer in Chrome or Edge with pop-ups allowed. Results are for information, and document images must be purchased.

Sellers can use the name search to see what stands against the property before listing: the vesting deed, open mortgages, an old lien that was paid but never discharged, or a death certificate that was never recorded. A buyer's title agent runs the same search, so a problem found early costs less time.

Anyone worried about deed fraud can enroll in the free property fraud alert at propertyfraudalert.com or by phone at 1-800-728-3858. It sends a notice whenever a document carrying the owner's name is recorded.

sections.h2: Where recording fits in a sale
sections.html:
It comes last. At closing the title agent collects the signed, notarized deed, pays the recording fee and any transfer tax, and sends the package to the county. Until the deed is recorded and indexed, the sale is not visible in the public record.

Property tax enters the same week. The year after a transfer, the new owner's taxable value is uncapped, and the buyer files a property transfer affidavit with the local assessor. Challenging an assessment starts at the March Board of Review in your city or township and can continue to the Michigan Tax Tribunal. Owners who need more time on summer taxes are sent by the county treasurer's page to the state's deferment rules.

A house with deferred repairs, back taxes or an estate behind it can sell for cash with no lender repair list. The recording steps are identical in every case, and the $30.00 fee is the same for a one-page quitclaim as for a long deed with exhibits. After the office indexes the instrument, ask your closing agent for the recorded deed and its recording details.

faqs.q: How much is recording in Lenawee County?
faqs.a: $30.00 per document, whatever the page count. Transfer tax is a separate charge that depends on the sale price.

faqs.q: Can Lenawee County staff draft my deed?
faqs.a: No. Staff do not provide forms and cannot advise on or complete a document for you. Hire a title agent or attorney to draft it.

faqs.q: Who pays Lenawee County transfer tax?
faqs.a: The seller, under MCL 207.523, with payment due to the county treasurer for the property's location. Settlement statements normally show it as a seller charge.

faqs.q: What is the cheapest way to get a deed copy?
faqs.a: Ask the county office itself. A counter copy is $1.00 per page, and a deed can run as little as $2.00, versus as much as $83.00 from commercial mailers.

faqs.q: Why would a Lenawee County deed be rejected?
faqs.a: Typical causes are photocopied signatures, narrow margins, a missing drafter address, names that differ from the notary block, or type that is too small. Compare the document against the county's 17-point list.
